title: Uganda Pushes First Oil to Mid-2027 as Iran War Holds Up Equipment | OilPrice.com

Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com.

Uganda’s dream to achieve its first commercial oil production and crude exports has been delayed yet again, extending the country’s wait to more than two decades since commercial oil reserves were first discovered in the country in 2006.

Officials from the Uganda National Oil Company (UNOC) and the Petroleum Authority of Uganda (PAU) have announced that Uganda’s first oil production and exports have now been pushed back to before the end of June 2027, blaming the delay on international supply chain bottlenecks and disruptions linked to the war in Iran. According to the PAU, the Middle East conflict delayed key equipment and material deliveries such as parts for metering, electrical instrumentation and telecommunications systems required to finalize the production and evacuation infrastructure.

The delay will create a rather substantial hole in the country’s budget, with Uganda’s Finance Minister Henry Musasizi telling parliament in June that the Ush 84.39 trillion budget for FY 2026/2027 had projected petroleum revenues of Ush 1.44 trillion (~$380 million).

According to Ugandan officials, while construction work at the $5.6-billion East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) is more than 90% complete, critical supporting facilities such as pump stations three and four and the pipeline’s electrical, instrumentation, telecommunications and security systems are still incomplete, requiring coordinated testing and commissioning across the EACOP, Tilenga, Kingfisher and Tanga projects. Lawmakers put the Tilenga Project at 78% complete and the Kingfisher development at 90% in October; however, the Central Processing Facilities (CPFs) required to treat and stabilize the raw crude are still undergoing final installation and pre-commissioning. Additionally, the 1,443-kilometre EACOP heated export pipeline linking western Uganda to Tanga Port in Tanzania requires the system to be thermally integrated to operate safely before any oil can move due to the waxy nature of Ugandan crude.

Uganda is projected to achieve a combined peak output of about 230,000 barrels of oil per day across TotalEnergies’ (NYSE:TTE) Tilenga project and CNOOC’s Kingfisher project. Production is expected to kick off with an initial rate of around 25,000 barrels per day from the Kingfisher field, rising to the field’s 40,000-barrel-per-day capacity, while Tilenga ramps up toward its 190,000-barrel-per-day peak. According to the Petroleum Authority of Uganda, the government will potentially earn between 1.5 and 2.5 billion dollars per year once oil production begins, a welcome new revenue stream for the East African country whose merchandise export earnings clocked in at ~$13.4 billion in 2025. Uganda is home to ~6.65 billion barrels of oil in place (OIP), with about 1.65 billion barrels estimated as recoverable.

The oil export delay has muddied Uganda’s financial outlook considerably, with S&P Global Ratings revising the outlook on the country’s B- sovereign credit rating from positive to stable. S&P projects Uganda’s fiscal deficit at 6.0% of GDP in fiscal year 2027. The Bank of Uganda had already raised its benchmark policy rate by 225 basis points to 12.0% at an emergency meeting in mid-October 2026 as the shilling slid, further tightening domestic financing conditions. Uganda’s heavy reliance on domestic debt issuance to plug budget gaps has pushed interest payments above a quarter of government revenue, with S&P projecting the share to approach 30%, while a less supportive external environment, higher global energy prices and lower coffee prices have weakened the country’s terms of trade and put pressure on the Ugandan shilling. S&P has lowered Uganda’s growth forecast for fiscal 2027 to 5.8%, down from earlier projections of 7.0% to 7.5% and a 6.4% expansion in fiscal 2026, with the growth outlook dampened by regional spillovers from Middle East disruptions, softer agricultural pricing and an Ebola-related slowdown in tourism.

That said, Uganda is just one of several East African countries looking to unlock their hydrocarbon resources, with neighboring Tanzania looking to start production at its massive offshore gas assets. Tanzania holds an estimated 57.5 trillion standard cubic feet (Tcf) of discovered natural gas, 47.13 Tcf of it in deepwater fields offshore. International energy companies including Shell (NYSE:SHEL), Equinor (NYSE:EQNR), and ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) are partnering with the state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) to build a $42 billion Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) export terminal in Lindi. This project will commercialize these offshore reserves, though host government agreements are still being finalized and a final investment decision remains pending.

Meanwhile, Nigeria’s oil tycoon and Africa’s richest man, Aliko Dangote, is moving ahead with plans to build a giant oil refinery at Lamu in neighboring Kenya, while Ethiopia inaugurated the first phase of its Ogaden Liquefied Natural Gas Project in October 2025, with a second phase planned to support 1,000 megawatts of power generation.
